title: Vector space
statement: A vector space over a field K is a set V with addition + : V × V → V and scalar multiplication · : K × V → V such that: (u + v) + w = u + (v + w), u + v = v + u, there is a zero vector 0 with v + 0 = v, every v has an additive inverse -v, and a(v + w) = av + aw, (a + b)v = av + bv, a(bv) = (ab)v, 1v = v for all a, b ∈ K and u, v, w ∈ V.

title: Subspace
statement: A subset U of a K-vector space V is a subspace if 0 ∈ U and U is closed under addition and scalar multiplication; equivalently U is nonempty and closed under all linear combinations.

title: Span
statement: The span of a set S in V is the set of all finite linear combinations of elements of S. It is the smallest subspace of V containing S.

title: Linear independence
statement: Vectors v₁, ..., vₙ are linearly independent if a₁v₁ + ... + aₙvₙ = 0 forces a₁ = ... = aₙ = 0. Otherwise they are linearly dependent.

title: Basis
statement: A basis of V is a linearly independent subset of V that spans V. Equivalently, every vector of V has a unique expression as a finite linear combination of basis vectors.
proof: An expression exists because the set spans V. It is unique exactly because of linear independence: if two expressions for the same vector differ, subtracting them gives a nontrivial linear relation.

title: Dimension
statement: The dimension of V is the cardinality of a basis of V; any two bases have the same size, so this is well defined. V is finite-dimensional if it admits a finite basis.
proof: If B has n elements and spans V, then any linearly independent set C has at most n elements: writing each c in the basis B and applying the exchange argument, |C| > n would make C dependent. Applying this in both directions to two bases gives equal sizes.

title: Linear map
statement: A map f: V → W between K-vector spaces is linear if f(v + w) = f(v) + f(w) and f(av) = a f(v) for all v, w ∈ V and a ∈ K; equivalently f preserves all linear combinations.

title: Kernel
statement: The kernel of a linear map f: V → W is ker f = {v ∈ V : f(v) = 0}. It is a subspace of V.
proof: f(0) = 0, so 0 ∈ ker f. If f(v) = f(w) = 0 then f(v + w) = 0 and f(av) = a f(v) = 0, so ker f is closed under addition and scalar multiplication.

title: Image
statement: The image of a linear map f: V → W is im f = {f(v) : v ∈ V}. It is a subspace of W.
proof: 0 = f(0) is in im f; f(v) + f(w) = f(v + w) is in im f; a f(v) = f(av) is in im f.

title: Rank
statement: The rank of a linear map f is rank f = dim im f. For a matrix, the rank is the dimension of the span of its columns.

title: Nullity
statement: The nullity of a linear map f is nullity f = dim ker f.

title: Rank-nullity theorem
statement: For a linear map f: V → W with V finite-dimensional, dim V = dim ker f + dim im f.
proof: Take a basis v₁, ..., vₖ of ker f and extend it to a basis v₁, ..., vₖ, vₖ₊₁, ..., vₙ of V. The images f(vₖ₊₁), ..., f(vₙ) span im f (replace each vector by its coordinates in the basis, then drop the kernel part) and are linearly independent: if a sum of them is zero, the corresponding combination of the v's lies in ker f, hence uses only v₁, ..., vₖ, and independence in V gives all coefficients zero. So they form a basis of im f and dim V = k + (n - k) = dim ker f + dim im f.

title: Matrix of a linear map
statement: Given a linear map f: V → W, a basis B = (b₁, ..., bₙ) of V and a basis C of W, the matrix [f] with respect to B and C has as j-th column the coordinates of f(bⱼ) in C. The coordinates of f(v) in C equal the matrix [f] times the coordinates of v in B.

title: Composition is matrix multiplication
statement: If f: V → W and g: W → X are linear maps with matrices M(g) and M(f) in fixed bases, then the matrix of the composition g ∘ f is M(g) M(f).
proof: The j-th column of M(g)M(f) is M(g) times the j-th column of M(f), which equals M(g) applied to the coordinates of f(bⱼ), i.e. the coordinates of g(f(bⱼ)) — the j-th column of the matrix of g ∘ f.

title: Change of basis
statement: Let B and B' be bases of V and let P be the matrix whose columns are the B'-coordinates of the vectors of B. Then the B-coordinates of any v equal P times the B'-coordinates of v, and for an endomorphism f the matrix in the basis B' equals P⁻¹ [f] P, where [f] is the matrix in the basis B.

title: Similar matrices
statement: Square matrices A and B are similar if B = P⁻¹ A P for some invertible matrix P. Similar matrices represent the same endomorphism in different bases.

title: Determinant
statement: The determinant det A of an n × n matrix is the signed volume scaling factor of the linear map; it is computed by cofactor expansion det A = ∑ⱼ ((-1)ⁱ⁺ʲ aᵢⱼ det(Aᵢⱼ)) along any fixed row i, with the determinant of a 1 × 1 matrix equal to its entry.

title: Determinant is multiplicative
statement: For square matrices A and B of the same size, det(AB) = det(A) det(B).
proof: For fixed A with det A not zero, the map B ↦ det(AB)/det(A) is alternating multilinear in the columns of B and equals 1 at B = I, hence equals det B by uniqueness of the normalized alternating multilinear form. The case det A = 0 follows by continuity (or by a similar argument), and both sides vanish.

title: Nonzero determinant iff invertible
statement: A square matrix A is invertible if and only if det A is not zero.
proof: If A is invertible then 1 = det I = det(A A⁻¹) = det(A) det(A⁻¹), so det A is nonzero. Conversely if A is not invertible its columns are dependent, a column operation makes one column zero, and the determinant is 0.

title: Invertibility equivalences
statement: For an n × n matrix A (equivalently an endomorphism of an n-dimensional space) the following are equivalent: A is invertible; ker A = {0}; A is injective; A is surjective; rank A = n; the columns of A are linearly independent; det A is not zero; 0 is not an eigenvalue of A.
proof: Rank-nullity gives: A injective iff ker A = {0}, and then nullity 0 so rank A = n = dim, so A is surjective; conversely rank A = n forces nullity 0 by rank-nullity. det A not zero iff invertible is the determinant criterion. 0 is an eigenvalue iff there is v ≠ 0 with Av = 0 iff ker A is nontrivial.

title: Eigenvalue and eigenvector
statement: A scalar λ is an eigenvalue of an endomorphism f: V → V if there is a nonzero v with f(v) = λv; such a v is an eigenvector. Equivalently ker(f - λ id) is nontrivial.

title: Eigenspace
statement: The eigenspace of f for an eigenvalue λ is ker(f - λ id); its nonzero vectors are the eigenvectors of λ, and its dimension is the geometric multiplicity of λ.

title: Characteristic polynomial
statement: The characteristic polynomial of a square matrix A (or endomorphism) is χ(t) = det(t I - A), a monic polynomial of degree n.

title: Eigenvalues are the roots of the characteristic polynomial
statement: λ is an eigenvalue of A if and only if χ(λ) = det(λ I - A) = 0.
proof: χ(λ) = 0 means λ I - A is singular, i.e. not invertible, so by the invertibility criterion ker(λ I - A) is nontrivial: there is v ≠ 0 with Av = λv. Conversely such a v makes λ I - A singular, so its determinant is 0.

title: Diagonalizable
statement: An endomorphism f (or matrix A) is diagonalizable if V has a basis of eigenvectors of f; equivalently A is similar to a diagonal matrix.

title: Eigenvectors of distinct eigenvalues are independent
statement: Eigenvectors corresponding to pairwise distinct eigenvalues of a linear map are linearly independent.
proof: Induct on m. Suppose a₁v₁ + ... + aₘvₘ = 0 with the vᵢ nonzero eigenvectors for distinct λ₁, ..., λₘ. For m = 1, a₁v₁ = 0 gives a₁ = 0. For m > 1, apply f - λₘ id to the relation: a₁(λ₁ - λₘ)v₁ + ... = 0 involves m - 1 vectors, so by induction all those coefficients vanish; distinctness gives a₁ = ... = aₘ₋₁ = 0, and then aₘvₘ = 0 gives aₘ = 0.

title: Criterion for diagonalizability
statement: An n × n matrix A is diagonalizable if and only if its characteristic polynomial splits into linear factors over K and for every eigenvalue the geometric multiplicity equals the algebraic multiplicity; equivalently the sum of the dimensions of the eigenspaces equals n.
proof: Eigenvectors from distinct eigenspaces are independent, so choose a basis of each eigenspace: their union is independent and spans the direct sum of the eigenspaces. It is a basis of Kⁿ exactly when the total dimension n is reached, which happens iff the geometric multiplicities add up to n; this is exactly when the characteristic polynomial splits and the geometric multiplicity equals the algebraic multiplicity.

title: Cayley-Hamilton theorem
statement: Every square matrix satisfies its own characteristic polynomial: χ(A) = 0, where χ(t) = det(t I - A).
proof: Over the complex numbers, triangularize A = P T P⁻¹; then χ(A) = P χ(T) P⁻¹, and χ(T) is upper triangular with diagonal entries χ(tᵢᵢ) = 0, hence zero. The general case follows by extending scalars or by a density argument.

title: Trace
statement: The trace of a square matrix is the sum of its diagonal entries: tr A = a₁₁ + ... + aₙₙ.

title: Trace and determinant are symmetric functions of the eigenvalues
statement: If χ(t) = (t - λ₁) ⋯ (t - λₙ) over the algebraic closure, then tr A = λ₁ + ... + λₙ and det A = λ₁ ⋯ λₙ, counted with algebraic multiplicity.
proof: Expand det(t I - A) along the diagonal: the coefficient of tⁿ⁻¹ is -(a₁₁ + ... + aₙₙ) = -tr A, and the value at t = 0 is det(-A) = (-1)ⁿ det A. Comparing with (t - λ₁) ⋯ (t - λₙ), whose tⁿ⁻¹ coefficient is -(λ₁ + ... + λₙ) and constant term is (-1)ⁿ λ₁ ⋯ λₙ, gives the claim.

title: Similar matrices share the characteristic polynomial
statement: Similar matrices have the same characteristic polynomial, hence the same determinant, trace and eigenvalues.
proof: det(t I - P⁻¹ A P) = det(P⁻¹ (t I - A) P) = det(P⁻¹) det(t I - A) det(P) = det(t I - A), using multiplicativity of the determinant.

title: Injectivity is a trivial kernel
statement: A linear map f is injective if and only if ker f = {0}.
proof: If f is injective and f(v) = 0 = f(0), then v = 0, so ker f = {0}. Conversely if ker f = {0} and f(v) = f(w), then f(v - w) = 0, so v - w = 0 and v = w.

title: A linear map is determined by its values on a basis
statement: Let b₁, ..., bₙ be a basis of V. Given any vectors w₁, ..., wₙ in W there is exactly one linear map f: V → W with f(bᵢ) = wᵢ for all i.
proof: Every v has a unique expression v = ∑ aᵢbᵢ, so define f(v) = ∑ aᵢwᵢ; uniqueness of the coordinates makes f well defined, and linearity follows from the rules for coordinates. Any linear map with those values must agree with this formula, so f is unique.

title: Inner product
statement: An inner product on a real vector space V is a map ⟨v, w⟩: V × V → ℝ that is symmetric (⟨v, w⟩ = ⟨w, v⟩), linear in each argument, and positive definite (⟨v, v⟩ > 0 for v ≠ 0).

title: Norm induced by an inner product
statement: The norm of v is ‖v‖ = √⟨v, v⟩; it satisfies ‖v‖ ≥ 0 with equality iff v = 0, and ‖av‖ = |a| ‖v‖.

title: Cauchy-Schwarz inequality
statement: For all v, w in an inner product space, |⟨v, w⟩| ≤ ‖v‖ ‖w‖, with equality if and only if v and w are linearly dependent.
proof: If w = 0 both sides are 0. Otherwise, for every real t, 0 ≤ ‖v + t w‖² = ‖v‖² + 2t⟨v, w⟩ + t²‖w‖². This quadratic in t is nonnegative everywhere, so its discriminant 4⟨v, w⟩² - 4‖v‖²‖w‖² is ≤ 0, giving the inequality. Equality holds iff the quadratic has a real root, i.e. v + t w = 0 for some t, i.e. v and w are dependent.

title: Triangle inequality
statement: For all v, w, ‖v + w‖ ≤ ‖v‖ + ‖w‖.
proof: Expand: ‖v + w‖² = ‖v‖² + 2⟨v, w⟩ + ‖w‖² ≤ ‖v‖² + 2‖v‖‖w‖ + ‖w‖² = (‖v‖ + ‖w‖)², using Cauchy-Schwarz for the middle term. Taking square roots gives the claim.

title: Orthogonality
statement: Two vectors v and w are orthogonal, written v ⊥ w, if ⟨v, w⟩ = 0. Orthogonal nonzero vectors are linearly independent.

title: Orthogonal complement
statement: The orthogonal complement of a subspace U is U⊥ = {v : ⟨v, u⟩ = 0 for every u ∈ U}. It is a subspace, and for finite-dimensional V, V is the direct sum of U and U⊥: every v decomposes uniquely as u + w with u ∈ U and w ∈ U⊥.
proof: Linearity of the inner product in the first argument shows U⊥ is a subspace. For the decomposition, take an orthonormal basis e₁, ..., eₖ of U, set u = ∑ ⟨v, eᵢ⟩ eᵢ, and check that v - u is orthogonal to every eᵢ, hence to U; uniqueness follows since a vector of U intersecting U⊥ must be orthogonal to itself, hence zero.

title: Orthogonal basis
statement: A basis b₁, ..., bₙ is orthogonal if its vectors are pairwise orthogonal. Then the coordinates of any v are ⟨v, bⱼ⟩/⟨bⱼ, bⱼ⟩.
proof: Take the inner product of v = ∑ aⱼbⱼ with bᵢ: ⟨v, bᵢ⟩ = aᵢ⟨bᵢ, bᵢ⟩ because all other terms vanish.

title: Orthonormal basis
statement: A basis is orthonormal if it is orthogonal and every basis vector has norm 1. Then ⟨eᵢ, eⱼ⟩ = 0 for i ≠ j and ⟨eᵢ, eᵢ⟩ = 1.

title: Gram-Schmidt process
statement: Every finite-dimensional inner product space has an orthonormal basis. Given any basis v₁, ..., vₙ, the Gram-Schmidt recursion u₁ = v₁, uₖ = vₖ - ∑ (⟨vₖ, uᵢ⟩/⟨uᵢ, uᵢ⟩) uᵢ, where the sum runs over i < k, produces an orthogonal basis with the same spans, and normalizing gives the orthonormal basis eₖ = uₖ/‖uₖ‖.
proof: Each uₖ is orthogonal to u₁, ..., uₖ₋₁ by construction (the subtractions remove all components along them), and uₖ is nonzero because vₖ is not in the span of v₁, ..., vₖ₋₁. So u₁, ..., uₙ are n pairwise orthogonal nonzero vectors, hence linearly independent, hence a basis; normalizing keeps orthogonality and gives norm 1.

title: Orthogonal projection
statement: For a subspace U with orthogonal basis u₁, ..., uₖ, the orthogonal projection of v onto U is proj(v) = ∑ (⟨v, uᵢ⟩/⟨uᵢ, uᵢ⟩) uᵢ. It is the unique point of U closest to v, and v - proj(v) lies in U⊥.
proof: The difference v - proj(v) is orthogonal to every uᵢ, hence to U. For any u ∈ U, the Pythagorean identity gives ‖v - u‖² = ‖v - proj(v)‖² + ‖proj(v) - u‖², which is minimized exactly at u = proj(v).

title: Expansion in an orthonormal basis
statement: If e₁, ..., eₙ is an orthonormal basis, then every v = ∑ ⟨v, eᵢ⟩ eᵢ and ‖v‖² = ∑ ⟨v, eᵢ⟩².
proof: Write v = ∑ aᵢeᵢ and take inner products with eⱼ: ⟨v, eⱼ⟩ = aⱼ by orthonormality. Then ‖v‖² = ⟨∑ aᵢeᵢ, ∑ aⱼeⱼ⟩ = ∑ aᵢ² = ∑ ⟨v, eᵢ⟩².

title: Orthogonal matrix
statement: A square matrix Q is orthogonal if QᵀQ = I. Equivalently its columns form an orthonormal basis, and Q preserves inner products and norms: ⟨Qv, Qw⟩ = ⟨v, w⟩.
proof: The (i, j) entry of QᵀQ is ⟨qᵢ, qⱼ⟩, which equals the Kronecker delta exactly when the columns are orthonormal. Then ⟨Qv, Qw⟩ = vᵀQᵀQw = vᵀw = ⟨v, w⟩.

title: Adjoint
statement: The adjoint of a linear map f on an inner product space is the map f* defined by ⟨f(v), w⟩ = ⟨v, f*(w)⟩ for all v, w. With the standard inner product on ℝⁿ, the matrix of f* is the transpose of the matrix of f.

title: Symmetric matrix
statement: A real square matrix A is symmetric if Aᵀ = A, equivalently A is self-adjoint: ⟨Av, w⟩ = ⟨v, Aw⟩ for all v, w.

title: Real symmetric matrices have real eigenvalues and orthogonal eigenvectors
statement: Every eigenvalue of a real symmetric matrix is real, and eigenvectors belonging to distinct eigenvalues are orthogonal.
proof: Let Av = λv with v ≠ 0. Then λ‖v‖² = ⟨Av, v⟩ = ⟨v, Av⟩ = (conjugate of λ)‖v‖², so λ equals its conjugate and λ is real. If Av = λv and Aw = μw with λ ≠ μ, then λ⟨v, w⟩ = ⟨Av, w⟩ = ⟨v, Aw⟩ = μ⟨v, w⟩, so (λ - μ)⟨v, w⟩ = 0 and ⟨v, w⟩ = 0.

title: Spectral theorem for real symmetric matrices
statement: Every real symmetric n × n matrix A is orthogonally diagonalizable: A = Q D Qᵀ with Q orthogonal and D real diagonal. Equivalently, ℝⁿ has an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors of A.
proof: Induct on n. A has a real eigenvalue λ with a unit eigenvector q. Because A is self-adjoint, the orthogonal complement of q is A-invariant: if ⟨v, q⟩ = 0 then ⟨Av, q⟩ = ⟨v, Aq⟩ = λ⟨v, q⟩ = 0. By induction that (n - 1)-dimensional space has an orthonormal eigenbasis; together with q it is an orthonormal eigenbasis of ℝⁿ.

title: Pythagorean theorem
statement: If v and w are orthogonal, then ‖v + w‖² = ‖v‖² + ‖w‖².
proof: ‖v + w‖² = ⟨v + w, v + w⟩ = ‖v‖² + 2⟨v, w⟩ + ‖w‖² = ‖v‖² + ‖w‖² since ⟨v, w⟩ = 0.

title: Rank and nullity of a projection
statement: The map f: ℝ² → ℝ², f(x, y) = (x, 0), has ker f = span{(0, 1)} (the y-axis), im f = span{(1, 0)} (the x-axis), rank f = 1 and nullity f = 1, consistent with rank-nullity: 2 = 1 + 1.
